paras: The lynching at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, took place in the early morning of October 30, 1903, when a mob took an unnamed Black man from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. He had been charged with entering the house of H. T. Allen to assault a member of the family, and no report gives his name. The story ran as a wire brief in papers from Mississippi to Minnesota, and the Hattiesburg paper later reprinted a Vicksburg comment counting it among recent examples of "swift justice."

According to a Hattiesburg dispatch, the man had entered Allen's house on the Monday night before the lynching, October 26, while Allen was away, "for the purpose of criminally assaulting a member of Mr Allen's family." A New Orleans wire gave the same charge and said he was then held in the Hattiesburg jail in the custody of the sheriff.

The mob gathered at about 1 o'clock in the morning. Its members went first to the depot "to see that no assistance was sent to the sheriff," then marched to the jail and broke it open in less than thirty minutes. They carried the prisoner half a mile from the jail and hanged him to a tree. The reports do not give the size of the mob or name any of its members.
No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The Daily Corinthian printed the Hattiesburg dispatch the same day under the headline "HANGED TO A TREE," and its weekly edition repeated it on November 4. The New Orleans wire reached northern papers within a day: the Minneapolis Journal ran it as "NEGRO IS LYNCHED," the Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier as "MOB HANGS NEGRO" with the deck "Mississippi Lynchers Defy Sheriff and Swing Up Prisoner," and the River Falls Journal folded one sentence into a news digest. Each of these items gave the charge as the reason for the lynching without questioning it.

On November 13 the Hattiesburg Daily Progress quoted the Vicksburg American, which cited the case as proof "that it is no trouble to get swift justice in the south" and described the victim as "strung up for climbing through the window of a room occupied by a white lady." The paragraph closed by remarking on "a determined movement to settle the overcrowded docket question," wording that can be read as approval or as sarcasm, and the Hattiesburg paper added no comment of its own. No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.

The accounts differ on the accusation's details: the Hattiesburg dispatch and the wire said he entered Allen's house to assault a family member, while the later Vicksburg paragraph said he climbed through the window of a white woman's room.

bases: A mob took an accused Black man from the Hattiesburg jail and hanged him to a tree (A1, A2, A3).

A mob broke open the jail, took out a prisoner charged with entering a house to assault a woman of the family, and hanged him to a tree half a mile away (A1, A3); a mob acting against an accused prisoner is a group of three or more acting under a pretext of justice (A2, A6).

A Hattiesburg-datelined report (A1) and a separate New Orleans wire (A2, A3) agree on the lynching and the accusation while giving different details, and the Vicksburg American, quoted by the Hattiesburg paper, also reports it (A6).

accounts.label: Hattiesburg dispatch
accounts.gist: The man who entered Allen's house Monday night to assault a family member was lynched by a mob early October 30; the mob gathered about 1 o'clock and acted quickly.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: The man was taken from the jail 'last night', after the mob guarded the depot against help for the sheriff and broke open the jail, and was hanged to a tree half a mile away.

accounts.label: Vicksburg American (quoted by Hattiesburg Daily Progress)
accounts.gist: A Black man at Hattiesburg was 'strung up' for climbing through the window of a room occupied by a white woman.
